Prepared by: Jose F. Meneses-Echávez. Collaborators: Rafael Nozal, Brita Askeland, Birgitte Klüwer, Anna Hayman R, Ingvild Kirkehei, Kjersti Rydland Department of Infectious Disease Control and Vaccines, Norwegian Institute of Public Health, Oslo, Norway Contact: jose.meneses\@fhi.no Date: 07.05.2026

# Key summary

This proof of concept represents the first validation of an AI-assisted workflow for literature selection within a living evidence map for the Adult Vaccination Program in Norway, referred to as LEVAK (in Norwegian, *Levende Evidenskart for Vaksiner*). LEVAK is intended to be an interactive living evidence hub covering the three vaccines included in the national program: COVID-19, influenza, and pneumococcal vaccines. It will also monitor research on attitudes toward vaccination and interventions for increasing vaccination coverage and influencing public attitudes toward vaccination.

This report evaluates the R package `AIscreenR` for title and abstract screening, using a health technology assessment (HTA) of herpes zoster vaccination (HZV) as a benchmark [@HZV_FHI2026]. Researchers at the Department of Infectious Disease Control and Vaccines at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health conducted the original manual screening of titles and abstracts. Their screening decisions serve as the reference standard for this proof of concept evaluation.

The unit of analysis for this validation consisted of 11,445 references retrieved by the HZV team from the databases included in the HTA [@HZV_FHI2026]. We prepared the reference library and developed prompts based on the selection criteria used in the HTA. To evaluate the performance of `AIscreenR`, we present a confusion matrix and report performance metrics, including accuracy and workload savings.

The screening results presented in this report are the product of an iterative process. An initial screening, referred to as HZV Screening 1, was conducted using a first draft of the prompt with GPT-4o-mini. Subsequently, a refined prompt was deployed in both GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini to compare their performance. Based on the results of this iteration, we then conducted HZV Screening 2 using both models.

The best screening performance was obtained using GPT-5-mini with the fine-tuned prompt, as follows:

**Key findings**

`AIscreenR` correctly identified 87% of the references included by the HZV team. This performance exceeds the 75% threshold recommended in the literature for implementation within evidence synthesis workflows [@vembye2025].

`AIscreenR` reduced the screening workload by nearly 82%. It safely identified and removed 9,337 references (82% of the total) that had also been excluded by the HZV team.

The LLMs tend to be over-inclusive, which allows researchers to safely double-check the data. `AIscreenR` included 1,972 references (17%) that were ultimately excluded by the HZV team. Consequently, the HZV team would have only needed to screen 2,079 out of the 11,445 total references to identify the 123 included studies.

**Conclusion**

`AIscreenR` should currently be utilized to prioritize screening rather than to replace human review entirely. This tool can safely be used as a second screener for title and abstract screening in an evidence synthesis, such as the one conducted by the HZV team. Fine tuning the prompts is crucial. The recall and specificity values align with the recommendations of Vembye et al. [@vembye2025] for a trustworthy an valid use of `AIscreenR` in evidence synthesis. Further validation studies will help us better understand the potential of `AIscreenR` in prioritizing vaccine research.

# Background

## AIscreenR

`AIscreenR` [@vembye2025] is an R package designed to streamline the title and abstract screening phase of evidence synthesis by deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) through the [OpenAI API](https://openai.com/nb-NO/api/). `AIscreenR` provides a communication interface between researchers and large language models (LLMs). Researchers instruct the LLM to assess the eligibility of a study by using a prompt that mirrors the selection criteria. It is most commonly used to reduce the immense manual workload of evidence synthesis, particularly by serving as an efficient "second reviewer" that can accurately identify and remove irrelevant studies [@vembye2025].

`AIscreenR`'s performance was validated in 2025, using as a benchmark the screening decisions from 22 high-quality systematic reviews with different levels of complexity [@vembye2025]. `AIscreenR` showed that the LLM performed on par with, and in some cases even better than, human reviewers in title and abstract screening [@vembye2025]. The tool demonstrated high accuracy and reliability, especially when a "human-in-the-loop" strategy was employed.

# Objective

To evaluate the performance of `AIscreenR` in screening references at the title and abstract level, using a health technology assessment on herpes zoster vaccination as the gold-standard comparative benchmark.\

# Methods

This proof-of-concept evaluation is conducted to better understand the performance of `AIscreenR` in title and abstract selection within evidence synthesis for vaccine research. We aim to deploy `AIscreenR` as the screener for relevant vaccine research to be mapped into a living evidence map (acronym: LEVAK). The methodological framework adheres to recent guidance presented by Cochrane [@Gartlehner2026].

As detailed in the full HZV report [@HZV_FHI2026], an experienced librarian searched in electronic databases by an experienced librarian. Pairs of researchers manually and independently screened the studies and resolved disagreements on inclusion via consensus. The final list of included and excluded studies was provided by the HZV project leader (Eli Heen) in a RIS file. The following sections of the document outline the data cleaning and preparation, as well as the `AIscreenR` pipeline used to execute the screening.

We constructed a confusion matrix to display the performance of `AIscreenR` compared to the final screening decisions from the HZV report [@HZV_FHI2026]. In evidence synthesis, the confusion matrix help us in [@ghosh2022a]:

- Error Analysis: Identifying misclassification patterns.

- Bias Detection: Understanding the balance between False Negatives (FN) and False Positives (FP).

- LLM Selection: Comparing different models based on their screening performance.

- Fine-tuning: Evaluating how the LLMs respond to different prompting approaches.

The confusion matrix visualizes the following metrics:

• True Positives (TP): The number of references correctly included by `AIscreenR` (i.e., references also included by the HZV team).

• True Negatives (TN): The number of references correctly excluded by `AIscreenR` (i.e., references also excluded by the HZV team).

• False Positives (FP): References incorrectly included by `AIscreenR` (Type I errors), meaning references included by `AIscreenR` but excluded by the HZV team.

• False Negatives (FN): References incorrectly excluded by `AIscreenR` (Type II errors).

True negatives (TN) are important for reducing workload, as they represent the number of references that a review team can avoid screening by using AIscreenR. In contrast, false negatives (FN) represent the relevant references that would have been missed without human verification.

Based on the confusion matrix, we then calculated the following metrics:

• **Recall** (Sensitivity, also known as true positive rate): The proportion of truly relevant studies correctly included by `AIscreenR`. Recall is the most critical metric; a target of \>90% ensures that study selection in LEVAK is safe and does not miss critical new evidence.

• **Specificity** (true negative rate): The proportion of truly irrelevant studies correctly excluded by `AIscreenR`. High specificity help researchers stay focused on relevant studies. If specificity is low, researchers will have to manually screen too many irrelevant papers (False Positives).

## Data requirements

For the `AIscreenR` screening functions to operate successfully, the dataset must contain at least three specific variables: a unique identifier for each record (e.g., `studyid`), the article `title`, and the `abstract`.

It is also highly recommended to include a `human_code` variable containing previous screening decisions (0 for excluded, 1 for included) in order to validate the AI’s performance.

## Data quality

Before the screening phase, users must ensure data quality by filtering out records with missing abstracts and resolving any character encoding issues that could interfere with the API's token processing in `AIscreenR`.

In many academic workflows, the search results will most likely be saved in an EndNote library before being brought into R. To facilitate the import, users should export their EndNote library as an XML or RIS file, as these formats are the most stable for preserving the relationship between titles and abstracts.

Once exported, the `synthesisr::read_refs()` function can parse these files directly, maintaining the metadata structure required for the screening process. This function belongs to the [`synthesisr`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/synthesisr/vignettes/synthesisr_vignette.html) package, which is a specialized tool for importing, exporting, and manipulating bibliographic data in R.

## HZV use case

On 30 January 2026, the research librarian (Marita Heintz) provided the literature search results in a RIS file (.ris) format. The results of the title and abstract screening for the original Herpes Zoster vaccine HTA were not available. Instead, Eli Heeen and Lene Juvet provided Jose Meneses with the final list of included studies and those excluded at the full-text stage.

To reconstruct the dataset for validation, Jose Meneses manually coded these references in EndNote to establish the following classifications:

- **Title and Abstract Screening (TA)**

  - Included references (`Included_TA`)

  - Excluded references (`Excluded_TA`)

- **Full-Text Screening (FT)**

  - Included references (`Included_FT`)

  - Excluded references (`Excluded_FT`)

After manually coding the `Included_TA` references in EndNote, we reconstructed the `Excluded_TA` set by subtracting the `Included_TA` references from the complete library of references. To replicate this in EndNote, follow these steps:

1.  Navigate to **Groups** \> **Create From Groups**.

2.  Name the new group (e.g., `Excluded_TA`).

3.  Under "Include References in," select the **All References** group.

4.  Set the operator to **NOT** and select the `Included_TA` group in the dropdown.

5.  Click **Create**.

### Human_code variable

The `human_code` variable allows us to validate `AIscreenR` 's performance, as it contains the screening decisions made by the HZV team (i.e., the human reviewers).

We manually created a new field in EndNote to assign human assessments to each reference. This `human_code` variable must be 0 for `Excluded_TA` and 1 for `Included_TA`. To add this variable to each reference in our RIS file, we must first create the custom field in EndNote using the following steps:

#### Step 1: Create the Field in Your References

To make a tag "global," you must first ensure the field exists within your database records.

1.  Go to **Edit \> Preferences** (Windows) **\>** Select **Reference Types** from the menu **\> Modify Reference Types**.

2.  Find one of the empty columns (such as `Custom 1`) and type the name you want (e.g., *human_code*).

3.  Click **OK**. All your references will now have this new field available.

#### Step 2: Bulk Fill the Field

If you want this field (tag) to appear across all existing references without typing them one by one:

1.  Select all your references (**Ctrl+A**).

2.  Go to the **Library** menu \> **Change/Move/Copy Fields**.

3.  In the **Change Fields** tab, select the field you just named (e.g., *Custom 1*).

4.  Choose the option **Replace whole field with:** and type the text you want to appear (e.g, 1 for `Included_TA`).

5.  Press **OK**.

6.  Repeat these steps for the `Excluded_TA`.

#### Step 3: Configure the RIS Export Format

EndNote does not export custom fields by default. You must instruct it to associate your new field with a RIS tag (such as `U1`).

1.  Go to **Edit \> Output Styles \> Edit "RefMan (RIS) Export"**.

2.  In the menu on the left, click on **Templates**.

3.  Locate the reference type you use most (e.g., *Journal Article*).

4.  You will see a list of tags like `AU  - Author`. Go to the end of the list and manually add:

    - Type `U1  -` and then click the **Insert Field** button to select your custom field (e.g., *Custom 1*).

5.  **Save your changes:** Go to **File \> Save As** and give it a name like `Custom RIS Export`.

#### Step 4: Exporting the edited RIS file

Ensure that when you clicked **File \> Export** in EndNote, you actually select the new "`Custom RIS Export`" style, rather than the default "RefMan (RIS) Export, to ensure the `U1` field is included in the final file.

### Adjustment to references (optional)

We restricted the database to the variables required by `AIscreenR`: ID, title, abstract, and `human_code`. The `human_code` variable is essential only when human screening results are available, as it enables a direct comparison between `AIScreenR`'s performance and the decisions made by human reviewers.

## AIscreenR workflow

The following is a step-by-step description of the workflow:

### Package and Data upload

It is practical to centralize all packages and functions used for the evaluation and reporting into a dedicated code chunk.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: 'hide'

#install.packages("rsconnect")
library(rsconnect)

# Load packages and libraries
library(AIscreenR)
library(writexl)
library(dplyr)
library(synthesisr)
library(tibble)
library(revtools)
library(flextable)
library(tinytex)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

library(future)

devtools::install_github("MikkelVembye/AIscreenR") # most recent pakcage updates

#Load data of the project
load(".RData")
```

### Set API Key

`AIscreenR` uses an API key to connect to a Large Language Model (LLM), in this case, the OpenAI API to connect to ChatGPT. After obtaining your API key (which is private and confidential), you can save it using the following code:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: false

# usethis::edit_r_environ() # Run this code to open your .Renviron file and  write CHATGPT_KEY=your_key. Thereafter, close and save the .Renviron file and restart RStudio (ctrl + shift + F10). From now on, the AIscreenR functions will automatically use get_api_key() to retrieve your API key from your R environment. 

get_api_key() # To check the API Key was saved successfully.
```

### Importing the dataset

To import references for `AIscreenR`, you typically utilize the `synthesisr` or `revtools` packages to convert standard bibliographic files—such as .ris, .bib, or .txt—into an R-compatible data frame. The process begins by reading the raw file into R, which generates a table where each row represents a unique study [@vembye2025].

We import the references that will be screened by `AIscreenR`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: false

confusion_helvetesild3_values<- read_excel("C:/Users/JOFM/OneDrive - Folkehelseinstituttet/Research projects/FHI/Smittevern/VVP/Helvetesild_testing/confusion_helvetesild3_excel.xlsx") #main file with the references (search results)

HZV_references<-confusion_helvetesild3_values %>% 
  select(ID, human_code, title, abstract, studyid)

View(HZV_references) #inspecting the references
save(HZV_references, file = "HZV_references.RData")
nrow(HZV_references)
save.image(file = ".RData")
```

### Missing titles check

Missing titles: Use the following code to ensure no references are missing a title.

```{r}
sum(is.na(HZV_references$title)) # check missing titles
```

All the references have a title (No titles missing).

### Missing abstract check

The abstract is the primary source of information used by the LLM to determine whether a study meets the inclusion criteria. `AIscreenR`, independent of the specific GPT model employed, tends to exclude references by default when information is insufficient. If a study without an abstract is actually relevant, it may result in a False Negative (key evidence is omitted from the synthesis).

Furthermore, the validation metrics for `AIscreenR` assume the LLM has access to the same data as a human reviewer. Empty abstract fields artificially lower the performance scores, leading to biased conclusions regarding the tool's validation.

The abstracts in the database show "No information" instead of "NA". Use this code to standardize the missing values to "NA":

```{r}
# Verify the "No information" items.
sum(HZV_references$abstract == "No information", na.rm = TRUE) 

# Convert "No information" to a real "NA".
HZV_references$abstract[HZV_references$abstract == "No information"] <- NA
```

We can check the number of missing abstracts now:

```{r}
sum(is.na(HZV_references$abstract)) # check missing abstracts
```

Abstracts are missing for 1,616 references, representing 14% of the 11,445 total entries in the EndNote library.

# **HZV screening 1**

This is our first, exploratory screening.

### Prompt (HZV screening 1)

The prompt is the set of instructions that the LLM follows to determine the relevance of each study. It must mirror the selection criteria, defining the key inclusion and exclusion criteria as clearly as possible. To ensure high accuracy, the prompt should be detailed and thorough.

You can draft the prompt in either R or Word before integrating it into the pipeline.

```{r}
# HZV_prompt <- "Role: You are an expert systematic review screener specializing in vaccinology and epidemiology. 
# Task: Evaluate whether a study meets the following specific inclusion criteria. 
# Population: Adults aged fifty years or older. Include participants regardless of previous vaccination history, history of herpes zoster, or presence of comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer’s). 
# Intervention: Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV) (e.g., Shingrix, HZ/su) or Zoster Vaccine Live (ZVL) (e.g., Zostavax). 
# Comparison/Control: Placebo, no vaccine, or an alternative vaccine (including head-to-head comparisons between RZV and ZVL). 
# Study Design: Included: RCTs, non-randomized studies, observational studies (prospective/retrospective cohort, registry-based, quasi-experimental, case-control, nested case-control), and post-marketing safety evaluations. 
# Secondary Research: Include systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and literature reviews. 
# Excluded: Case studies and case series. 
# Evaluation Rule: Does the study meet all the inclusion criteria? Only include the study if every criterion is satisfied."
```

# Results (HZV screening 1)

### Exploring the screening results

Print the results of the screening done by `AIscreenR`. Check the following variables:

- **decision_gpt:** the raw gpt decision - either "1", "0", "1.1" for inclusion, exclusion, or uncertainty.

- **detailed_description:** the detailed description of the given decision made by OpenAI’s GPT API models.

- **decision_binary:** the binary gpt decision, that is 1 for inclusion and 0 for exclusion.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| results: false

HZV_screening <- readRDS("HZV_screening.rds") # load the screening results

# Preview of the screening results data.
view(HZV_screening$answer_data) # inspect the data

# Distribution of LLM-generated screening decisions
HZV_screening$answer_data %>%  
  count(decision_binary)

#Saving the results file
saveRDS(HZV_screening, "HZV_screening.rds")
```

`AIscreenR` excluded 10,227 references and included 1,214.

We found that *four* references were marked as 'NA' by the software. We checked these manually and reclassified them as excluded (0) as they are not deemed relevant to the study.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| results: false

#Assign 0 to the references with NA (n=4)
HZV_screening$answer_data$decision_binary[is.na(HZV_screening$answer_data$decision_binary)]<-0

#Check
HZV_screening$answer_data %>%  
  count(decision_binary)
```

After cleaning the data, `AIscreenR` excluded 10,231 references and included 1,214 references @tbl-HZV-screening-rawtable.

```{r}
# Data wrangling_row data (first table)
HZV_screening_rawtable <- HZV_screening$answer_data %>%
  count(decision_binary) %>%
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(decision_binary == 1, "Included", "Excluded"),
    Percentage = n / sum(n)
  ) %>%
  select(Decision, n, Percentage)
view(HZV_screening_rawtable)

# Saving the object in R and also as Excel
saveRDS(HZV_screening_rawtable, "HZV_screening_rawtable.rds")
writexl::write_xlsx(HZV_screening_rawtable, "HZV_screening_rawtable.xlsx")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-HZV-screening-rawtable
#| tbl-cap: "AIScreenR screening results"
#| message: false
#| echo: false

# 1. We assign the gt object to the variable name
HZV_screening_rawtable_gt <- HZV_screening_rawtable %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "AIScreenR screening results",
    subtitle = "Distribution of AIScreenR Screening Results"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Decision = "Decision",
    n = "Frequency (n)",
    Percentage = "Percentage (%)"
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = Percentage,
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Note: Four references returned an error in AIScreenR; these were manually reviewed and categorized as excluded"
  ) %>%
  opt_stylize(color = "blue", style = 1)

# 2. Display the table in the report
HZV_screening_rawtable_gt

# 3. Save the table to your outputs folder
# Make sure to include the file extension (.png, .pdf, or .html)
gtsave(HZV_screening_rawtable_gt, "outputs/HZV_screening_rawtable.png")
```

Now that the data are clean with unique values of either included and excluded by `AIscreenR`, we can proceed to the analysis.

## Analyzing the results

`AIscreenR` (and other AI tools) is seen as a diagnostic tool, detecting relevant references for the review question and excluding irrelevant ones. There are two primary entries: the binary inclusion/exclusion decisions made by the HZV team (human reviewers) and those made by `AIscreenR`. This comparison results in a 2x2 table, which we refer to as a 'Confusion Matrix' [@ghosh2022a].

### Confusion matrix

To prepare the key metrics for the confusion matrix, we retrieve the raw data (the distribution of decisions made by both `AIscreenR` and humans), organize these into a data frame, and then generate the confusion matrix table.

1.  Retrieve and prepare the raw data.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Preparing the raw data for the metrics:
HZV_confusion <- table(
  Human = HZV_screening$answer_data$human_code,
  AI = HZV_screening$answer_data$decision_binary
)
```

2.  Organize the data in a data frame.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false 

# Converting the raw data of the confusion matrix to a data frame (mandatory step in dplyr)
HZV_confusion_df <- as.data.frame(HZV_confusion)
colnames(HZV_confusion_df) <- c("human_code", "decision_binary", "n")

HZV_confusion_final <- HZV_confusion_df %>% # using the dataframe (df)
  mutate(
    Human = if_else(human_code == 1, "Included", "Excluded"),
    AIscreenR = if_else(decision_binary == 1, "Included", "Excluded")
  ) %>%
    pivot_wider(id_cols = Human, names_from = AIscreenR, values_from = n)
```

3.  Plotting the confusion matrix table.

The evaluation of the HZV screening process (n = 11,445 references from the searches) is shown in @tbl-confusion-matrix.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-confusion-matrix
#| tbl-cap: "Confusion matrix AIscreenR vs HZV team"
#| echo: false

HZV_confusion_final %>%
  mutate(Human = factor(Human, levels = c("Included", "Excluded"))) %>%
  arrange(Human) %>%  # This puts "Included" row first
  select(Human, Included, Excluded)%>%  # Reorder columns to put "Included" first
  gt(rowname_col = "Human") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Confusion matrix AIscreenR vs HZV team",
    subtitle = "Performance analysis in study selection"
  ) %>%
  tab_stubhead(label = "Human reviewers") %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "AIscreenR",
    columns = everything()
  ) %>%
  
  # Add the "Total" row
  grand_summary_rows(
    columns = everything(), # use all columns
    fns = list(Total = ~sum(., na.rm = TRUE)), #sum function
    fmt = list(~fmt_number(., decimals = 0))
  ) %>%
  opt_stylize(color = "blue", style = 1)

# Saving the Excel file for this table.
writexl::write_xlsx(HZV_confusion_final, "HZV_confusion_final.xlsx")
```

Interpreting the results:

- **True Negatives (TN)=** 10,171 references (88.9%) were correctly excluded by both the HZV team and `AIscreenR`. In other words, `AIscreenR` safely removed 89% of the irrelevant records.

- **False Negatives (FN) =** 48 references (0.4%) included by the HZV team but missed by `AIscreenR`.

- **True Positives (TP) =** 75 references. These are the relevant studies correctly identified by both HZV team and `AIscreenR`.

- **False Positives (FP) =** 1,138 references were included by `AIscreenR` but excluded by the HZV team. This represents the *"residual manual workload"* (i.e., the 1,138 papers the review team still needs to check manually to ensure they are truly irrelevant).

### Key performance metrics

Based on the key performance metrics in the confusion matrix, we can now estimate the accuracy and the recall.

#### Recall (Sensitivity)

Recall represents the proportion of truly relevant references that were correctly identified and included by `AIscreenR`. This is critical metric as it measures the `AIscreenR`'s ability to find "all the needles in the haystack." A high recall ensures that no relevant studies are missed during the screening process.

#### Accuracy

Accuracy is the proportion of all decisions made by `AIscreenR` (both inclusions and exclusions) that were correct. While informative, accuracy can sometimes be misleading in systematic reviews if the number of irrelevant papers vastly outweighs the relevant ones (class imbalance).

The `screen_analyzer` function in `AIscreenR` calculates both recall and accuracy @tbl-HZV-performance.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: false

# Run the analyzer function to estimate the metrics
HZV_analysis<-screen_analyzer(HZV_screening, human_decision = human_code)
View(HZV_analysis)
HZV_analysis

# Saving the analysis of the screening results
saveRDS(HZV_analysis, "HZV_analysis.rds")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-HZV-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Performance metrics of AIscreenR results"
#| message: false
#| echo: false

# Create the table
HZV_analysis %>%
  select(model, recall, specificity) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Performance metrics of AIscreenR results",
    subtitle = "Comparative performance of AIscreenR in screening references at the title and abstract level on herpes zoster vaccination as the gold-standard comparative benchmark"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    model = "gpt-4o-mini",
    recall = "Recall (Sensitivity)",
    specificity = "Specificity"
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(recall, specificity),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(80),
    heading.background.color = "#2c3e50"
  ) %>%
  opt_stylize(color = "gray", style = 6)
```

#### Specificity

Specificity measures the proportion of truly irrelevant references that were correctly excluded by `AIscreenR`. Unlike Recall that focuses on finding what is relevant, Specificity focuses on accurately "clearing out" the noise. High specificity reduces the number of irrelevant references that researchers must manually double-check.

#### Workload Savings

Workload savings quantifies the efficiency gain provided by `AIscreenR`, expressed as the percentage of the total references that the review team no longer needs to screen manually because `AIscreenR` correctly excluded. This metric directly reflects the time and resource reduction achieved by implementing `AIscreenR`.

@tbl-keymetrics presents the key performance metrics of `AIscreenR` in screening the studies compared to the HZV team.

| Performance metric | Value | Interpretation |
|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| Recall (Sensitivity) | 61.0% | The most vital metric for quality. It shows that `AIscreenR` captured 61% of the relevant references. The remaining 39% (the 48 False Negatives) were missed. |
| Accuracy | 89.5% | The overall proportion of correct decisions (both inclusions and exclusions) made by `AIscreenR`. While high, accuracy can be misleading in imbalanced datasets. |
| Specificity | 89.9% | The ability of `AIscreenR` to correctly identify and discard irrelevant studies. A 90% specificity is excellent for significantly narrowing down a large library. |
| Workload savings | 89.4% | The "Efficiency Gain." It measures the percentage of the total library that the HZV team was able to skip screening entirely thanks to `AIscreenR.` |

: Key performance metrics in screening of AIScreenR vs HZV team

# Conclusions (HZV screening 1)

- `AIscreenR` should be used to prioritize screening rather than replacing human review entirely.

- `AIscreenR` identified 61% of the references included by the HZV team, meaning it overlooked 48 relevant studies. This recall should be higher (at least 75% before full implementation in evidence synthesis workflows).

- `AIscreenR` resulted in a workload reduction of nearly 90% during the tittle and abstract screening of the 11,445 references retrieved from the databases.

- The HZV team could have safely excluded 90% of the total references by using `AIscreenR`.

# False Negative Analysis

To address the low recall observed in the initial `AIscreenR` screening, we must analyze the False Negatives (FNs) to identify potential improvements for the prompt. The FNs are those relevant studies that `AIscreenR` excluded but the humans had included.

A refined prompt should, in theory, improve `AIscreenR`’s recall by providing the LLM with clearer inclusion and exclusion boundaries.

## Select the False Negatives

The unit of analysis at this stage consists of all False Negatives identified in the screening confusion matrix. We must create a dedicated variable containing these FNs to systematically inspect the exclusion reasons provided by `AIscreenR` @tbl-confusion-matrix.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Create the groups in the confusion matrix: TP, TN, FN, FP
HZV_screening_excel <- read_excel("C:/Users/JOFM/OneDrive - Folkehelseinstituttet/Research projects/FHI/Smittevern/VVP/Helvetesild_testing/HZV_screening_excel.xlsx")

HZV_confusion<- HZV_screening_excel%>%  # new object
  mutate(result_type = case_when(
    human_code == 1 & decision_binary == 1 ~ "True Positive (TP)",
    human_code == 0 & decision_binary == 0 ~ "True Negative (TN)",
    human_code == 0 & decision_binary == 1 ~ "False Positive (FP)",
    human_code == 1 & decision_binary == 0 ~ "False Negative (FN)"
  ))
view(HZV_confusion)
saveRDS(HZV_confusion, "HZV_confusion.rds")

# Extract the FNs from "HZV_confusion"
HZV_FN<- HZV_confusion%>%
  filter(result_type== "False Negative (FN)") 
view(HZV_FN)
# This is the new variable containing all the False Negatives(FNs).

writexl::write_xlsx(HZV_FN, "HZV_FN.xlsx")
saveRDS(HZV_FN, "HZV_FN.rds")
```

With the False Negatives now stored in an object called 'HZV_FN', we will export this dataset to review the exclusion reasons provided by `AIscreenR` (column "detailed_description"). This analysis will directly inform the necessary refinements to our screening prompt.

## Tuning the prompt

Analysis of the exclusion reasons revealed that `AIscreenR` incorrectly excluded references that did not specify the vaccine type, did not limit participants to a specific age group, focused on vaccine safety and studies on varicella/chickenpox vaccines.

The revised and tuned prompt is now saved as a new variable in our R environment.

```{r}
HZV_prompt_tuned<-"Role: You are an expert systematic review screener specializing in vaccinology and epidemiology. 
Task: Evaluate whether a study meets the following specific inclusion criteria. 
Population: Adults of any age (18 years and older), with a specific focus on including middle-aged, older adults, and the elderly (e.g., 60–70 years, 80+ years, and beyond). Include individuals regardless of:  
Vaccination History: Including those with or without a previous history of vaccination (e.g., varicella/chickenpox). 
Medical History: Including those with or without prior episodes of herpes zoster. 
Health Status: Including participants with or without existing comorbidities or chronic conditions. This encompasses healthy populations as well as participants with conditions such as cardiovascular disease, organ or stem cell transplantation, Alzheimer’s disease, or other immunocompromising factors. 
Intervention: Studies evaluating the effectiveness and safety of either the Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV; e.g., Shingrix, HZ/su), the Zoster Vaccine Live (ZVL; e.g., Zostavax), or unspecified zoster vaccines, such as those evaluated in national vaccination programs. 
Comparison/Control: Placebo, no vaccine, or alternative vaccines (including head-to-head comparisons between RZV and ZVL). 
Study Design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized studies, and observational studies (prospective/retrospective cohort, population-based, registry-based, quasi-experimental, case-control, and nested case-control). Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and post-marketing safety evaluations are also eligible. 
Exclude the following: Commentaries, narrative reviews, case studies, and case series. 
Evaluation Rule: Does the study meet all the inclusion criteria? Only include the study if every criterion is satisfied.
If you are uncertain about the inclusion of a study or if the study shows signs that the full text might meet the inclusion criteria,
choose INCLUDE to minimize the risk of missing relevant studies."
```

**Analyzing the results**

To evaluate the impact of the tuned prompt, we measured the reduction in False Negatives (FNs). This is calculated by subtracting the new FNs (tuned) from the FNs in the initial screening. This equals the prompt's effectiveness in capturing previously missed relevant references, thereby improving recall.

```{r}

```

- The previous number of FNs in HZV_confusion_final was 48.

- HZV_tuned_screening = `AIscreenR` using GPT-4o-mini included 29 (TPs) references and excluded 19 references (FNs).

- FN reduction = 29 references (60% FN reduction rate).

The fine-tuned prompt reduced the FNs rate by 60%.

## False Negative analysis using GPT-5-mini

We evaluate the comparative performance of OpenAI’s recent model, GPT-5-mini, which is optimized for high-volume requests and offers greater speed than GPT-4o-mini. According to OpenAI’s technical documentation [@openai_models_docs], GPT-5-mini excels in efficiency, featuring a 400K token context window, which is a significant increase over the 128K window found in GPT-4o-mini. Newer models will be tested in future updates of this work.

To validate the performance of GPT-5-mini in controlling false negatives (FNs), we re-ran the original prompt on the identified FN cases and switched the model variable to GPT-5-mini, and compared the results.

```{r}

#| output: false
#| message: false

HZV_FN_gpt5_screening$answer_data %>%  
  count(decision_binary) #Checking the raw numbers

view(HZV_FN_gpt5_screening$answer_data) # inspect the data

#Saving the results file
saveRDS(HZV_FN_gpt5_screening, "HZV_FN_gpt5_screening.rds")
```

GPT-5-mini included 33 FN references (69% FN reduction rate), relative to the 29 references included by GPT-4o-mini (60% FN reduction rate). This represents a 9% screening performance gain.

3.  Plotting the confusion matrix

The evaluation of the **HZV screening 2 using** **gpt-4o-mini** (n = 11,445 references from the searches) is shown in @tbl-confusion-matrix2_gpt4omini.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-confusion-matrix2_gpt4omini
#| tbl-cap: "Confusion matrix AIscreenR vs HZV team - tuned prompt using gpt-4o-mini"
#| echo: false

HZV_confusion2_final %>%
  mutate(Human = factor(Human, levels = c("Included", "Excluded"))) %>%
  arrange(Human) %>%  # This puts "Included" row first
  select(Human, Included, Excluded)%>%  # Reorder columns to put "Included" first
  gt(rowname_col = "Human") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Confusion matrix AIscreenR vs HZV team - tuned prompt",
    subtitle = "Performance analysis in study selection"
  ) %>%
  tab_stubhead(label = "Human reviewers") %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "AIscreenR",
    columns = everything()
  ) %>%
  
  # Add the "Total" row
  grand_summary_rows(
    columns = everything(), # use all columns
    fns = list(Total = ~sum(., na.rm = TRUE)), #sum function
    fmt = list(~fmt_number(., decimals = 0))
  ) %>%
  opt_stylize(color = "blue", style = 1)

# Saving the Excel file for this table.
writexl::write_xlsx(HZV_confusion2_final, "HZV_confusion2_final.xlsx")
```

Interpreting the results of **HZV screening 2 using gpt4-o-mini**:

- **True Negatives (TN)=** 10,038 references (88%) were correctly excluded by both the HZV team and `AIscreenR`. In other words, `AIscreenR` safely removed 89% of the irrelevant records.

- **False Negatives (FN) =** 27 references (0.2%) included by the HZV team but missed by `AIscreenR`.

- **True Positives (TP) =** 96 references. These are the relevant studies correctly identified by both HZV team and `AIscreenR`.

- **False Positives (FP) =** 1,271 references were included by `AIscreenR` but excluded by the HZV team. This represents the residual manual workload (i.e., the 1,271 papers the review team still needs to check manually to ensure they are truly irrelevant).

# **Conclusion**

The comparison of GPT-4o mini and GPT-5 mini using the fine-tuned prompt in both models revealed higher recall for GPT-5 mini (87%) compared with GPT-4o mini (78%), whereas specificity was slightly higher for GPT-4o mini (89%) than for GPT-5 mini (83%). This also translated into greater workload savings with GPT-4o mini (89% vs. 82% with GPT-5 mini).

This proof of concept suggests that LLMs can be safely used to prioritize relevant studies during title and abstract screening of HZV vaccine research. We will use GPT-5 mini in our literature selection pipelines as part of the Living Evidence Map of Vaccine Research (LEVAK). The same pipeline presented in this document will be used for subsequent validations in the diseases included in LEVAK: influenza, COVID-19, and pneumococcal disease.

# Stability assessment of AIscreenR performance

The LLMs may give different answers over time, and these differences in the screening decisions affect the robustness of the studies included in LEVAK. This analysis aims to evaluate the stability of the screening decisions made by `AIscreenR` by comparing the results from previous iterations with ewer ones to assess their similarity. We hypothesized that `AIscreenR` maintains a stable performance over time when using the same set of references and the same judgments from content experts.

## Stability assessment 1

#### Second iteration using GPT-5-mini

This assessment was conducted by Jose Meneses on October 15, 2026.

**Step 1: Splitting the references into chunks**

We first split the entire set of references (11, 445 references) into manageable chunks to optimize processing and efficiency.

```{r}
chunks <- split (HZV_references,
    ceiling(seq_len(nrow(HZV_references))/200))

length(chunks)        # nr of chunks
nrow(chunks[[1]])     # must be 200
```

**Step 2. Creating a folder to store chunks**

```{r}
# # # creating the folder (directory)
dir.create("screening_chunks", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

**Step 3. Setting up the loop**

This loop processes all the chunks in sequence, with *i* being the chunk number. The function `sprintf("chunk_%03d.rds", i)` names the files (screened chunks) using a three-digit zero-padded format (e.g., `i = 1` will be `chunk_001.rds`, and `i = 12` will be `chunk_012.rds`).

```{r}

# for (i in seq_along(chunks)) {
#     f <- file.path("screening_chunks", sprintf("chunk_%03d.rds", i))  # naming the files
#   if (file.exists(f)) next       # skips completed iterations
```

**Step 4. Screening pipeline**

`tryCatch(A, error = B)` means “try A, and if it produces an error, do B instead of stopping all of R”.

- Part A is the same `tabscreen_gpt()` call we used in previous screenings, but with `data = chunks[[i]]`. It thus screens only that single chunk.

- Part B is a function that runs if an error occurs (for example, the text/html error). It prints a message stating which chunk failed and what the error was (`conditionMessage(e)`), and returns `NULL` (nothing). The result, whether it is a real result or `NULL`, is saved in `res`.

